title: Data Engineering, Machine Learning and Model Evaluation
summary: Building MealSenseAI's food classifier: two public datasets merged into one 320-class taxonomy, audited for leakage and conflicting labels, and used to fine-tune EfficientNet-B0 on a self-hosted GPU — reaching 70.6% top-1 and 85.7% top-3 accuracy on 45,800 held-out test images.
meta: Python · PyTorch · EfficientNet-B0 · CUDA · Docker · FastAPI · PostgreSQL
Ubuntu Linux · NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM)

paragraphs: MealSenseAI estimates the nutrition of everyday meals from a photograph, with a focus on Singaporean and Southeast Asian dishes that general food datasets cover poorly. It combines computer vision, transfer learning, nutrition-database mapping and small language models (SLMs).
This work produced its classifier: one model over a unified food taxonomy, built from two public datasets whose labels were harmonised and whose quality was checked before any accuracy was measured.
Two labelled image datasets pair international coverage with Singapore-specific dishes.
Combined: 310,861 images and 334 class entries, harmonised into 320 classes — broader coverage than either source alone, especially for food eaten in Singapore.
Every image was checked for integrity and duplication.

blocks.label: Why it matters.
blocks.text: A duplicate that lands in both training and test leaks the answer and inflates accuracy; duplicates with conflicting labels teach the model contradictions. Both have to be found before a score means anything.

paragraphs: The two datasets name foods differently — Food-101 writes "chicken_wings", FoodSG-233 "chicken wing". Their 101 + 233 = 334 class entries describe 320 distinct foods: 14 appear in both sources and were merged into one class each, so the model learns one dumpling, not two competing ones.

paragraphs: Reviewing the saved evaluation outputs surfaced two issues that change how the scores should be read:

items: A per-dataset scoring bug: macro-F1 for each source was averaged over all 320 classes, so every class a source doesn't contain counted as zero and Food-101 read 0.24. Averaged over its own 101 classes it is 0.75 (FoodSG-233: 0.67). The chart pipeline now computes it correctly.

An unexplained gap: the training, validation and test splits total 306,668 images — 4,193 fewer than the 310,861 audited — and the evidence does not record whether the 728 cross-split duplicate groups were among those removed. Until confirmed, test scores are treated as possibly slightly optimistic.

paragraphs: The classifier uses transfer learning on EfficientNet-B0, an architecture that balances accuracy against compute. Training ran in two stages: first only a new classification head over frozen ImageNet features, then the top of the network itself.

paragraphs: Images were split 232,713 for training, 28,155 for validation and 45,800 held back for the final test. Both experiments share a fixed seed and the same augmentation, applied to training images only.

blocks.label: Why top-3 matters.
blocks.text: The app shows its best guesses and the person confirms or corrects. With the right food among the first three 85.7% of the time, a correction is usually one tap.

blocks.caption: Singapore dishes are harder: more classes, fewer images for many of them, and many look alike.

blocks.caption: 275 classes score F1 ≥ 0.5; a tail of 45 does not.

blocks.title: Most frequent confusions
blocks.caption: Most are labels that overlap in meaning, not visual failures: a taxonomy problem as much as a vision one.

blocks.title: Confidence calibration
blocks.caption: Each point is a confidence band: when the model says 80%, it is right about 80% of the time. It errs slightly toward caution in the middle bands.

paragraphs: Calibration is what makes confidence usable in the product: 35% of test images were predicted with at least 90% confidence and those were right 97.3% of the time, so a threshold can decide when to accept a prediction and when to ask the person.

blocks.label: Caveat.
blocks.text: Whether the 728 cross-split duplicate groups were removed before splitting is not recorded (see Data processing, step 4), so these test scores may be slightly optimistic until that is confirmed.

paragraphs: Each run records its dataset partitions, architecture and checkpoint, configuration, epoch-level metrics, evaluation outputs, runtime and GPU performance, with timestamps — so any result can be reproduced and traced.
The classifier is one stage of a modular inference pipeline. The person confirms or corrects each prediction before it counts.

Keeping inference separate from application services lets detection, classification or nutrition analysis improve without redesigning the app. The aim is diabetes-aware insight — carbohydrate awareness and meal composition — as estimates, not medical advice.

items: Consolidated two datasets — 310,861 images — into a 320-class taxonomy
Audited integrity and duplication, exposing potential leakage and label conflicts
Reached 70.6% top-1 and 85.7% top-3 accuracy on 45,800 held-out images, at 0.69 ms per image
Showed the model is well calibrated (ECE 2.3%), so its confidence can drive when to ask the person
Validated GPU-accelerated training on a self-hosted CUDA workstation with consumer hardware
Designed a modular architecture linking computer vision, nutrition data and SLM explanations

paragraphs: Good machine learning is more than choosing and training a model: dataset quality, consistent labels, reproducible experiments, efficient compute and integration into the product matter as much. The largest confusions here came from the taxonomy, not the network.

Image-based nutrition estimation has real limits — mixed dishes, irregular portions and foods that look alike. Next: a hierarchical taxonomy for overlapping labels, longer fine-tuning while validation is still improving, confirmation that the test split is free of duplicates, better multi-food segmentation and portion estimation, and validation against independently labelled images.
